claim: One-step default inferences with generics are near ceiling for 2024 frontier models zero-shot (Claude 3 Opus 96.51, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 96.01, GPT-4 93.52 over 15 uncontroversial patterns), but a rule-list format (LogicBench non-monotonic: GPT-4 74.4 yes-label / 84.8 no-label) is much harder; the level depends on task format.
agent_test: Run both formats (generic sentence versus explicit default-rule list) on our agent at equal tokens and report the gap.

claim: Models fail to retract a conclusion when a defeater arrives: Belief-R update accuracy is near 0 to 35 percent for most open models (Llama-3 70B: update 10.99 vs maintain 92.09), and DeReLab shows GPT-5.1 correct on only 3.5 percent of defeating updates (gap 0.935, OR 891). Gap search: the failure is stubbornness, not noise; strong models intrude on irrelevant updates only about 1 percent (GPT-5.1 0.9, Gemma-4-31B 0.3), small models 15 to 36 percent.
agent_test: Feed multi-turn weakening updates; measure retract rate versus maintain rate with and without an S5 'check the defeater' step, same token budget.

claim: Models can label an update as weakening yet keep the old conclusion on the same turn (GPT-5-mini 95.4 percent labelled vs 20.3 percent revised; Llama-3.1-70B 85.1 vs 14.9). Gap search: the gap is partly a question-order effect. Asking the conclusion first helps the label (Gemma-4-31B 0.970 to 0.264 when the label comes first); label-first also raises the bias gap (Qwen3-32B 0.670 to 0.816). So a label-then-restate step is not supported and may hurt.
agent_test: Ask the conclusion question first, then the effect label. A/B test label-first-then-restate against conclusion-first at equal tokens; check GPT-5.x and Claude, which the order test did not cover.

claim: Default and belief-revision results are sensitive to wording and question order: wording variants correlate 0.99 with the base prompt in two cases but break in another; reversing question order drops the effect-label score (Gemma-4-31B 0.970 to 0.264); hearsay framing lowers update size by 2 to 5 points.
agent_test: Evaluate the agent on 3 paraphrases and both question orders; require stable answers before trusting a revise decision.

claim: Chain-of-thought and extended thinking have no consistent effect on default reasoning: CoT lowered mean accuracy 11.14 points in strong models (Kirkpatrick), changed Belief-R by about 1 point, and extended thinking removed the retraction bias in Qwen3-32B (gap 0.670 to 0.008), while more effort worsened a strict-rule condition in ArgGYM (50.8 to 11.7 percent). Gap search: no 2025-2026 Claude run of Belief-R, DeReLab or the Kirkpatrick set was found; Claude Opus 4.6/4.7 data exist only for nested-exception rule tasks (d01).
agent_test: Test revise with and without long reasoning at equal tokens, per model, on defeater items; do not assume more reasoning helps.

claim: Models treat generics as near-universals: accuracy on the defeasible wording correlates negatively (r below -0.6 in 6 of 8 patterns) with accuracy on the deductive wording, and irrelevant exemplars push agreement with a generic below 50 percent in several open models.
agent_test: Probe with 'usually' versus 'always' pairs and with irrelevant context; check the agent keeps rules defeasible but stable.

claim: Offloading default reasoning to a logic-programming solver beats direct LLM answering: bAbI 80.34 to 99.99 percent (GPT-3 + ASP), MultiLogicNMR 59.0/52.9 to 90.5/81.0 (skeptical/credulous), LOGicalThought +5.5 percent on defeasible reasoning; a monotonic SMT coupling scores near chance (35.8/35.0). The first two results share an author group.
agent_test: Give the agent a small ASP or Prolog tool for default rules; compare with plain reasoning at equal tokens.

claim: An external error signal is what makes revision work: solver feedback lifts LLM+ASP from 54.6 to 78.0 percent, while intrinsic self-correction without a signal lowers accuracy (GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 89.0; GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 41.8) and oracle labels raise it.
schema_part: G (doubt only on a signal) / S5
agent_test: Compare revise-on-signal versus revise-always at equal tokens; the signal can be a verifier, a failed test or a new observation.

claim: Humans suppress valid modus ponens when a second conditional adds a requirement (Byrne: 96 to 38 percent). Replications keep the direction but vary the size (Dieussaert 88/93/60; open answers N=10: 100/100/40). Answer format and sample drive the size.
agent_test: Not an agent test; use as the human baseline for additional-requirement items in Belief-R-style sets.

claim: When unsure, people cite concrete counterexamples more than probabilities, and known counterexamples lower confidence less for valid than invalid arguments (d=.187 vs .325).
agent_test: Add a 'name one counterexample' prompt only when a signal is present; compare with a probability-estimate step.

claim: Fine-tuned defeasible-NLI classifiers reach human level (RoBERTa 81.6/78.3/86.2 vs human 83.6/78.2/87.6), but update-only input already gets 65 to 72 percent, so part of the score is annotation artefact; an inference graph adds 1.4 to 3.4 points.
agent_test: Treat delta-NLI scores with caution; run an update-only control.

claim: Accuracy falls as conflict rate rises in older models (BoardgameQA conflict 0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.8; BERT near random at medium and high), but 2026 reasoning models are strong without tools (84.7 percent), so ASP added nothing there. Gap search: break-even depends on task type. Models alone are weak at computing answer sets (ASPBench exact match 23.2 percent average, 55.7 for deepseek-r1), and a rule engine still beat Claude and GPT-5.4 on nested-exception tasks (vendor paper).
agent_test: Run BoardgameQA at several conflict rates on our agent; a saturated benchmark gives no signal.

claim: Models accept coherent, congruent counter-evidence and resist incongruent evidence: ChatGPT, GPT-4 and PaLM2 mostly kept the original answer under entity-substitution counter-memory but yielded to coherent generated evidence; DeReLab found congruent-versus-incongruent gaps in 17 of 19 cells.
agent_test: Test updates that are coherent versus bare; check that the agent weights by source quality, not fluency.

claim: Generating exceptions for a generic is hard and noisy: exception precision@1 is 0.632 for the best generator and 0.839 after NLI filtering (+20.7 points); NLI labels between a generic and its exception are not clean contradictions.
agent_test: Test 'list exceptions then filter with a check' against 'list exceptions' alone at equal tokens.

claim: Rule memories with confidence edits improve agents: ExpeL on ALFWorld 'put' goes from 50 (ReAct) to 83 percent with ADD/EDIT/UPVOTE/DOWNVOTE insights plus retrieval; Hypotheses-to-Theories gains 10 to 30 points over CoT, and wrong rules cause 65 percent of CoT errors on CLUTRR. Gap search: the ExpeL vote is a count (start 2, drop at 0), so one counterexample lowers a rule by one and writes no exception; exceptions are untested.
agent_test: Store defaults with a count and a downvote on exception; compare with a flat note list at equal tokens.

claim: Current models can propose exception rules over scientific theories, but failures are mostly format: of 1,054 failures, 652 were contract violations, 366 token caps and 36 semantic misses. The panel is solvable by entity-local repair, so it does not show good exception scope. Gap search: DeFAb v2 (Oct 2026) reports that simple symbolic repairs solve all 336 tasks and 2 of 6 deployments are perfect, so the benchmark does not test exception scope; the feedback and token-cost studies are planned only.
agent_test: Measure the agent's output-format failure rate before judging its logic.

claim: Layering a gradual argumentation framework over LLM-written arguments gave no clear gain over chain-of-thought (accuracy about 0.54 to 0.81 across methods), and on structured argument tasks complete-task success is far below local partial correctness (Qwen3.5-27B: 88.7 native vs 35.8 percent complete).
agent_test: Test whether an argument-graph step adds accuracy at equal tokens; expect little.

claim: The formal families agree on the core: conflicting defaults give multiple extensions (Nixon diamond), skeptical reasoning accepts only what all extensions share, specificity overrides general defaults, and propositional default logic is Sigma2P/Pi2P-complete. Sources are McCarthy plus reviews, not Reiter's original.
agent_test: Encode 'more specific rule wins; on a tie, do not conclude' in the schema and test on Nixon-style items.

claim: Model size does not predict default-reasoning rank: Gemma 2 9B (92.69) beat 27B and Gemini Flash beat Pro; few-shot helps weak models (+28.74 Llama 2 7B) and hurts the strongest (Claude 3 Opus -6.81).
agent_test: Do not copy prompts across models; check few-shot per model.

claim: When the update is cleanly irrelevant, strong models almost never revise wrongly (intrusion: GPT-5.1 0.9 percent, Gemma-4-31B 0.3, Qwen3-32B with thinking 0.2) while small models do (Llama-3.1-8B 36.2, Llama-3.1-70B 15.2). Over-flip is also low in DeltaLogic small models (0 to 0.10). The main loss is the stale answer.
agent_test: Log stale, over-flip and abstain separately for the agent. Check whether the revise-on-signal gate raises over-flip on plausible but misleading facts, not only clean irrelevant ones.

claim: Pushing a model to re-check or to treat rules as exception-friendly buys misses back at the price of false revisions: an unconditional 'Are you sure?' lowers accuracy in every model (46 percent flip rate, 17 point average drop); an exception-aware prompt on Claude Opus 4.6 cut false negatives 7 to 4 but added 20 false positives (89.7 to 64.7 percent); models that update more drop on keep-the-conclusion items (Mixtral BU 35.38 / BM 36.57).
schema_part: S5 / G (doubt only on a signal)
agent_test: Test gated revise (defeater named first) against re-check-always at equal tokens on a default task set; score misses and false revisions separately.

claim: In 2026 the strongest Claude and GPT-5 models are at ceiling on single-level exceptions (43/43) but still fail nested three-level exception chains in some cells, and a cell can move without a version change (Opus 4.6 spacecraft 89.7 percent in March, 98.5 percent in April; GPT-5.4 construction 96.6 to 100). Source is a vendor paper.
agent_test: Pin model snapshots in any benchmark and re-run the exception-chain set on the deployed model before trusting a scaffold effect.

claim: Explicit priority and exception rules in the prompt give 63 to 86 percent verdict accuracy on the HOLMES law set, but traces skip most of the conflict-resolution rules (recall falls as conflicts rise while accuracy stays flat). No study compares explicit Reiter-style rules with plain-language generics at equal tokens.
agent_test: Run the same default set in three forms: plain generics, explicit unless-rules, explicit rules with a specificity order; score verdict and use of the full rule chain.

claim: The Nixon diamond appears only inside an aggregate in the one LLM study found: Claude-family models above 80 percent, GPT-4 family from below chance to 100 percent, forced yes/no. No study tests a skeptical withhold instruction or credulous choice. The search summary claim that models do not abstain under conflict came from a forced-choice paper with no abstain option.
agent_test: Build a 20-item conflict set with an undetermined option; score withhold, credulous pick and refusal with and without a withhold instruction.

claim: No evidence found for the remaining gaps: a label-then-restate repair (the reversed order hurt), single-case exception learning in ExpeL-style memory (update is a count), token cost of a solver tool call, and human default-inheritance numbers (Elio, Pelletier, Hewson and Vogel not opened).
agent_test: These need own experiments; do not cite literature for them.
